analysis.investment_thesis: CEAT operates in a capital-intensive, commodity-driven tyre business where 10.3% revenue CAGR over 9 years translated into a pitiful 0.9% net profit CAGR — the classic hallmark of a business with no pricing power cannibalised by input cost inflation. At 24x trailing P/E with borrowings nearly doubling in FY25 to ₹3,114 Cr, you are paying a fair-business price for a commodity manufacturer with thin, volatile margins.
key_strengths: ROCE of 15.4% just clears the minimum quality threshold, with strong FY24 EBITDA of ₹1,690 Cr indicating the business can generate decent returns when rubber prices cooperate
Revenue has grown consistently from ₹5,484 Cr (2016) to ₹13,218 Cr (2025), showing CEAT is gaining market share against global tyre majors in a large domestic market
OCF positive all 5 years, peaking at ₹1,719 Cr in FY24, demonstrating the business is not a capital trap in normal years
key_risks: Net profit CAGR of only 0.9% over 9 years despite 10.3% revenue growth exposes severe margin compression — the business is essentially running on a treadmill in real terms
Borrowings nearly doubled from ₹1,792 Cr (FY24) to ₹3,114 Cr (FY25), while FCF collapsed from ₹852 Cr to ₹149 Cr — an ominous signal about the new capex cycle
Finance costs compounding at 11.9% CAGR, materially faster than revenue or profit, silently destroying shareholder value over time
red_flags: No durable competitive moat — tyre manufacturing is deeply commoditised with MRF, Apollo, Michelin, and Bridgestone competing on identical products; CEAT has no pricing power whatsoever
FCF/Net Income ratio of only 32% (₹149 Cr FCF vs ₹471 Cr net profit in FY25) signals poor earnings quality — capex of ₹943 Cr almost entirely consumes operating cash flow

Operating margin of 9% in FY25 down from the FY24 peak of ~13.8% shows extreme sensitivity to natural rubber and petrochemical inputs — this is not a business, it's a raw material processing spread trade
analysis.detailed_analysis:
CEAT is a reasonable second-tier tyre company in a mediocre business. The tyre industry is structurally unattractive — raw materials (natural rubber, carbon black, steel) are globally priced commodities, OEM customers have enormous bargaining power, and replacement market competition is intense. The 9-year record is damning: ₹5,484 Cr of revenue became ₹13,218 Cr, but net profit of ₹436 Cr in 2016 is essentially ₹471 Cr in 2025 — nine years of effort producing near-zero wealth creation for owners. The borrowing surge in FY25 to fund new capacity (CWIP has been consistently high) means the equity return profile will likely worsen before it improves.

ROCE of 15.4% passes the minimum Munger bar but reflects a single strong year (FY24) rather than a durable structural advantage. The RPG Enterprises promoter group (47.21%) has been a credible steward, but this is an average business in a structurally challenged sector. At 24x trailing P/E and P/B of 3.3x, the market is pricing in optimism that the raw material cycle stays benign — that is a bet, not an investment.
